newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Far East Gold - Demand perks up, market nervous.
newsitem.headline: Far East Gold - Demand perks up, market nervous.

text.p: Physical gold demand perked up in Asian markets as prices continue to slide, but strong demand is being countered by selling, largely from Australian producers, dealers in Hong Kong and Singapore said on Friday.

"Just this morning when gold traded below $377.50 there were calls from everywhere," said Anderson Cheung, chief bullion dealer at Swiss Bank Corp.'s office in the British colony, when asked about physical demand.
Spot gold was trading at $377.50/378.00 an ounce at 1230 (0430 GMT) in Hong Kong on Friday, slightly below New York's previous $377.90/378.40 close on Thursday.
Dealers in Hong Kong and Singapore reported brisk sales from Australian producers on Thursday and Friday.
"We're seeing more Aussie producer sales," said one Hong Kong gold dealer on Friday.

Gold is also being pressured by losses in silver with the December silver futures contract contract on the New York Comex market trading at $4.760 an ounce on Thursday, the lowest level for the December contract in two years.
Spot silver also saw a low of $4.78 an ounce in the U.S., the lowest level since March 1995.
"Market sentiment in the precious metals is bad, with more downside potential in both gold and silver," said a senior precious metals trader at an international bank in Hong Kong.
Spot silver had strong support at $4.75-4.77, he said.
Some gold traders said that after the initial wave of physical gold purchases, when the price stepped below $379, buyers were getting nervous as the gold drop showed little sign of abating.
"Gold could well test $375 next week and then we're getting into territory that's been uncharted for a long time," said one gold dealer.
But if gold tumbled to $375 and held there for a day or two, buyers' confidence would be restored, the dealer said.
"It (demand) has been steady. But after buying, most people in Asia have gone out again and want to see if the price can come down further," one bank trader in Singapore said.
Demand had come largely from Indian gold buying ahead of the Diwali festival next week, Singapore-based traders said.
Strong physical demand lent support to the gold price, but could not stop a further drop in the face of strong sales, Hong Kong and Singapore dealers said.
Singapore gold premiums were quoted in a range between 35-50 U.S. cents an ounce slightly above last week's 30-50 U.S. cents, traders said.
It is too early to make a firm forecast for gold demand ahead of the Chinese New Year holiday in early February 1997 and beyond, gold traders said.
"It's too early to tell, everyone is very price sensitive," Swiss Bank Corp.'s Cheung said.
Gold demand in Asia traditionally picks up in the fourth quarter of the year, continuing into the early months of the coming year before tailing off.
